## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="a22-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Five measures</dt><dd>One number per goal: cost, CO₂, unserved energy, the low-income share of home bills, the gas share.</dd>
<dt>Definitions</dt><dd>Each measure is a choice of unit, boundary and formula; Fair and Secure most of all.</dd>
<dt>Unbeaten plans</dt><dd>No other plan is at least as good on all five goals and better on one: 8 of the 9 plans here, comparing values as shown.</dd>
<dt>Weights</dt><dd>How much each goal counts; people set them, and different weights pick different plans.</dd>
<dt>Limits</dt><dd>Caps on some goals; the solver finds the cheapest plan that meets them on seven weeks, or reports that none exists. The full year then checks it.</dd>
<dt>Who decides, who pays</dt><dd>Households and businesses pay through the tariff; a regulator or council approves; people downwind bear harm outside the cost.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Reading a radar honestly</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li><b>Scales are choices.</b> Rim (best) and center (worst): cost $100M and $250M a year; CO₂ 0 and 850 kt; unserved energy 0 and 2,000 MWh; low-income share 20% and 35%; gas share 0% and 100%.</li>
<li><b>Equal weights carry a price.</b> One spoke of cost ($150M) counts as much as one spoke of CO₂ (850 kt): about $176 a tonne, set by the scales, not by anyone's judgment of harm (<a href="12-trade-offs.html">lesson 12</a>: weights carry units).</li>
<li><b>Squeezed spokes.</b> Under a fixed charge per home, every plan's low-income share lies between 31.3% and 34.6%, so Fair scores span only 0.03 to 0.25: a weight on Fair barely moves a pick.</li>
<li><b>Shape, not area.</b> Reordering the spokes changes a polygon's area; compare plans spoke by spoke.</li>
<li><b>Ties as shown.</b> Verdicts treat values that round to the same shown number as equal. Under the income-graduated charge, C's share (21.61%) and D's (21.63%) both show 21.6%, so D beats C; at full precision, C is unbeaten.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Other ways to measure fairness, security and reliability</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li><b>Fairness as burden.</b> <span class="lx-term" data-term="energy-burden">Energy burden</span> is the share of income spent on home energy: electricity, gas and other fuels, not transport.</li>
<li><b>DOE's numbers.</b> DOE's LEAD tool puts it at about 6% for low-income U.S. households and 2% for others (2018–2022 data). DOE uses a different definition here: income up to 80% of the local median.</li>
<li><b>Not in this model.</b> Burden needs incomes and whole bills, which this town model does not have.</li>
<li><b>Security as diversity.</b> A supply is concentrated when one source makes most of it, and diverse when many sources make similar shares.</li>
<li><b>Diversity indices.</b> Shannon's and the Herfindahl index turn every source's share into one number; the Herfindahl index is the sum of the squared shares, 1 when one source makes everything. Stirling (2010) adds how different the sources are.</li>
<li><b>Reliability over many years.</b> Loss-of-load expectation counts shortfall hours over many weather years with random plant failures (<a href="a05-adequacy.html">A5</a>).</li>
</ul>
<p>Reviews of energy decisions with several criteria (Wang and co-authors, 2009) find cost, emissions, reliability and social measures in most studies, each defined in many ways.</p>
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Five goals as a model</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

Write each goal as a number to make small, $f_k(x)$ for $k = 1, \dots, 5$. The lesson's tools, in words:

- **Dominance.** Plan $x$ beats plan $y$ when $f_k(x) \le f_k(y)$ for every $k$ and $f_k(x) < f_k(y)$ for at least one.
- **Adding a goal.** It can rescue a beaten plan. It can beat a plan that was unbeaten only if another plan tied that plan on every earlier goal.
- **Weighted sum.** Each goal gets a score on its scale and a weight; the pick has the highest weighted total. With every weight above zero, the pick is unbeaten.
- **Clipping.** A value beyond its scale's end scores the same as that end, which can hide a difference, so the page weighs only the unbeaten plans.
- **Limits.** Step 7 asks for the cheapest plan with caps on CO₂, the gas share and the low-income share: the [epsilon-constraint]{.lx-term term="epsilon-constraint"} method, then a check on the full year.

The low-income share, worked out for a plan whose fixed costs are 95% of its cost:

| Tariff | Low-income homes pay | Their share of home bills |
|---|---|---|
| Fixed charge per home | 34.7% of the fixed costs, 29.6% of the running costs | 34.7% × 0.95 + 29.6% × 0.05 = 34.4% |
| Income-graduated (half the charge) | 21.0% of the fixed costs, 29.6% of the running costs | 21.0% × 0.95 + 29.6% × 0.05 = 21.4% |
| Per kWh only | 29.6% of every cost | 29.6% |

Same plan, same costs: the tariff alone moves the share by 13.0 points.

Mavrotas (2009) shows how to sweep the limits. Next: [M6](m06-carbon-in-models.qmd) (carbon in models) and [M12](m12-city-model.qmd) (a city model with screening fairness outputs).

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="a22-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="winall" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “With five goals, a good plan can usually win on all of them.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Here the cheapest plan (A) emits the most, and the cleanest (I) costs more than twice as much; no plan is best on all five.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="rescue" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Adding a goal can turn a beaten plan into an unbeaten one.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. Here 4 plans beaten on cost and CO₂ alone are unbeaten on all five. The reverse needs a tie: a new goal can beat an unbeaten plan only if another plan matched it on every earlier goal.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="measured" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A fairness score is measured, just as CO₂ is.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It rests on a tariff. With an income-graduated fixed charge, plans with more building cost (here the cleaner ones) have the lower low-income share, and E, F and G become beaten.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="a22">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="cd" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">Plans C and D differ only by 80 MW of gas peakers, which never ran in 2025. Which measure can tell them apart in C's favor?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">A reserve margin</li><li data-value="b">Unserved energy</li><li data-value="c">CO₂ a year</li><li data-value="d">The gas share</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>A <span class="lx-term" data-term="reserve-margin">reserve margin</span>: it counts capacity at the peak, 88% for C against 70% for D. The other three see the same year for both.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
<div id="a22-practice">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Practice · about 20 minutes on your own</p>
<p class="lx-hint">Use the nine plans' table at the top (a fixed charge per home; Reliable as unserved energy, Secure as the gas share).</p>
<ol class="lx-fb-practice">
<li><p><b>Is plan B beaten?</b> H costs less than B ($116.2M against $119.5M) and emits less (424 kt against 521 kt).</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Unbeaten: H leaves 1,605 MWh unserved and B none, so no plan matches B on all five.</p></details></li>
<li><p><b>Which plan beats plan C?</b></p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>D: it costs $5.9M less and is the same on the other four goals.</p></details></li>
<li><p><b>Measure Reliable by the reserve margin: is C still beaten?</b> C's margin is 88%, D's 70%.</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>No: C is now better on one goal, so D no longer beats it.</p></details></li>
<li><p><b>Plan D's total under equal weights.</b> Its scores: Cheap 0.63, Clean 0.83, Reliable 1.00, Fair 0.05, Secure 0.82.</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>0.666, the average of the five: the highest of the nine, so Equal weights picks D.</p></details></li>
<li><p><b>Give weights that pick plan D, not plan A.</b> Bills first (cost 40, clean 5, reliable 20, fair 30, secure 5) picks A.</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>For example cost 30, clean 30, reliable 20, fair 10, secure 10: D wins. Someone else's weights could still pick A.</p></details></li>
<li><p><b>A plan's fixed costs are 60% of its cost.</b> What share of home bills do low-income homes pay with a fixed charge per home, and with the income-graduated charge (21.0% of the fixed charges)?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>32.6% and 24.4%: the tariff alone moves the share by 8.2 points.</p></details></li>
</ol>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-real">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">In the real world</p>
<ul>
<li><b>Fairness:</b> DOE's <a href="https://www.energy.gov/cmei/scep/low-income-energy-affordability-data-lead-tool">LEAD tool</a> maps energy burden, with low income as up to 80% of the local median.</li>
<li><b>Security:</b> the <a href="https://www.ferc.gov/sites/default/files/2021-12/Cold%20Weather%20Report_%202021_120821.pdf">FERC–NERC report</a> on February 2021 traced plant outages to freezing and to gas supply.</li>
<li><b>Choosing:</b> which yardstick to use, and how much each counts, is decided by people.</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div class="lx-card lx-sources">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Sources and further reading</p>
<ul>
<li>EIA (2023, revised 2024). <a href="https://www.eia.gov/consumption/residential/data/2020/c&amp;e/pdf/ce2.1.pdf">2020 Residential Energy Consumption Survey, Table CE2.1</a> (PDF): homes and electricity use by household income.</li>
<li>U.S. DOE. <a href="https://www.energy.gov/cmei/scep/low-income-energy-affordability-data-lead-tool">Low-Income Energy Affordability Data (LEAD) Tool</a>.</li>
<li>FERC, NERC and Regional Entities (November 2021). <a href="https://www.ferc.gov/sites/default/files/2021-12/Cold%20Weather%20Report_%202021_120821.pdf">The February 2021 Cold Weather Outages in Texas and the South Central United States</a> (PDF), pp. 15–16.</li>
<li>Wang, J.-J., Jing, Y.-Y., Zhang, C.-F. and Zhao, J.-H. (2009). <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rser.2009.06.021">Review on multi-criteria decision analysis aid in sustainable energy decision-making</a>. Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews 13(9), 2263–2278.</li>
<li>Stirling, A. (2010). <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.enpol.2009.02.023">Multicriteria diversity analysis</a>. Energy Policy 38(4), 1622–1634.</li>
<li>Mavrotas, G. (2009). <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.amc.2009.03.037">Effective implementation of the ε-constraint method in Multi-Objective Mathematical Programming problems</a>. Applied Mathematics and Computation 213.</li>
<li>Technology costs, fuel prices and the 2025 weather: as listed in <a href="13-capstone.html#sources">lesson 13's sources</a>.</li>
```
